## The study question

This study estimates the excess Medicare payments in the 12 months after cryptococcosis is diagnosed among adult kidney transplant recipients, compared with similar recipients at the same time since transplant who have not been diagnosed.

- **Population:** adult kidney transplant recipients in the United States [with fee-for-service Medicare as their primary payer]{.pending}.
- **Comparison:** each case is compared with up to two recipients who have reached the same time since transplant without being diagnosed.
- **Outcome:** Medicare payments, month by month, from three months before diagnosis to the end of the twelfth month after it.
- **Measure:** the average excess payment per case over the 12 months after diagnosis.

**Decision pending:** whether other payer arrangements, such as Medicare as secondary payer, are ever eligible ([D1](quarto/analysis-plan.qmd#13-open-decisions)).

The data come from the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), which links transplant registry records to Medicare claims [@usrds2025guide].

## Why it matters

Cryptococcosis is uncommon after kidney transplant [@george2017epidemiology; @pappas2010transnet], but it is serious: in a national USRDS cohort, 22% of kidney recipients hospitalized for it died within six months [@fiorica2025mortality]. Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis lasts at least 10 weeks [@merry2016flucytosine]. Published US cost estimates are of single hospital stays, of modelled treatment, or of costs over time without a comparison group. We found no study that estimates the excess Medicare payments attributable to cryptococcosis over the months after diagnosis in kidney transplant recipients. [Clinical background](quarto/background.qmd) sets out the evidence.

## Study timeline and cost trajectories {#study-timeline}

@fig-cost-timeline illustrates how the planned study windows relate to case and control costs. The 365-day eligibility lookback is longer than the monthly cost-outcome window. Disease-related care and diagnostic workup can raise costs before the recorded diagnosis, so the prediagnosis trajectory is part of what the study aims to describe.

![Conceptual study timeframes and mean cost trajectories; no patient data or study estimates are shown. The monthly outcome panel spans days −90 to 359. Earlier dashed curves provide context outside that panel. Shaded differences are illustrative and do not establish causal attribution.](quarto/assets/integrated-cost-timeline.svg){#fig-cost-timeline width=100% fig-alt="Line diagram of mean costs over time for cases and controls. The eligibility bar spans days minus 365 to minus 1. Pale dashed curves precede the cost-outcome window. During intervals minus 3 to minus 1, cases rise above zigzagging controls, peak near the case diagnosis or matched control index date, and decline gradually while remaining higher through interval 11."}

[Open the figure at full size](quarto/assets/integrated-cost-timeline.svg).

For cases, time zero is the first qualifying diagnosis claim; controls are aligned at the same time since their most recent transplant, so their calendar dates may differ. The figure explains the intended windows, not the completeness of observation: coverage loss, death, and partial months require the handling specified in the [analysis plan](quarto/analysis-plan.qmd). Earlier costs may also inform planned matching covariates; they are outside the monthly outcome panel shown here.

## Methods

Each patient diagnosed with cryptococcosis (a *case*) is compared with up to two similar recipients who have reached the same time since transplant without being diagnosed (*controls*). Cases and controls are followed for 12 months from the same starting point, and the difference in their Medicare payments is the excess cost of cryptococcosis.

The [Study design and methods](quarto/study_overview.qmd) pages set out who is studied, how cases are found, how controls are matched, how costs are built and how they are analysed, with what the plan specifies and where the code stands.

## Reproducibility

The complete source code for the analysis, tables and figures is public in the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/VagishHemmige/Cryptococcus-cost-analysis). The script `R/main.R` runs the other scripts in order. Model assumptions, parameter values and the workflow are documented in the repository for transparency and reuse. The USRDS data are restricted, so the analysis can be rerun only by an analyst with authorized access to them.

[Braces](https://forum.posit.co/t/curly-braces-around-package-name-convention/122547) identify R packages throughout this site.
